brief.head: Tyrannies leak
brief.text: Authoritarian regimes are full of obedient people who hate the ruler, Ajay Shah said, which makes them rich ground for human intelligence, or HUMINT. {015-C01}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on CR Rao and his world
lead.head: Counting on Calcutta
body: Late in the Second World War, the Allies needed to know how many heavy tanks Germany made each month. Spies, the people “who knew the girlfriend of some brigadier”, said about 1,500. Statisticians, reading the serial numbers on destroyed tanks, said about 200.
After the war, Germany’s own production records showed the statisticians were right. “The moral of the story,” Amit Varma said, “is brigadiers lie to their girlfriends.” {015-J01}
“Or that tanks don’t lie,” Ajay Shah replied.
The tanks were only a warm-up for Shah’s tribute to his hero, the statistician CR Rao, who had died days before they recorded.
## A hero made in Calcutta

Rao, born in 1920, came from Andhra Pradesh to Calcutta as an ordinary student at PC Mahalanobis’s Indian Statistical Institute. It was before independence, with no government money; Mahalanobis often paid from his own pocket.
Cut off from the European mainstream, Rao produced two of what Shah counts among the greatest results of 20th-century statistics: the Cramér-Rao lower bound, in 1943, and the Rao-Blackwell theorem.

The first sets a limit on how good an estimator, a formula for inferring an unknown, can ever be. “You can run and run and build better and better estimators,” Shah said, “but you can’t cross the Cramér-Rao lower bound.” {015-C02}

Shah sees Rao as the product of an Indian ecosystem, more like the chess player Anand than Ramanujan, and so the greatest achievement of the Bengal Renaissance. Varma happily agreed: “You know the whole world is Bengali.”

Rao’s name survived, Shah said, thanks to the statistician Ronald Fisher, who visited the institute, grasped the results and began calling them by both names. “And suddenly for the whole world, it became Rao’s work.” {015-S03}
## Bullets and bombers

Varma answered with British planes. Returning aircraft had more bullet holes in the fuselage than in the engine. Abraham Wald asked: where are the missing bullets? In the planes that never came back, so the engine was what needed protecting. {015-S06}
Shah named the trap survivorship bias, then raised Varma with Allied bombers over Germany.

Pilots wanted to fly at 20,000 feet, out of reach of the guns, but from there very few bombs hit. Counting lives lost per factory destroyed, the statisticians, a young Robert McNamara among them, chose 6,000 feet.
## A survey and a planner

Varma then turned to Mahalanobis, reading from Nikhil Menon’s *Planning Democracy*. In 1944, measuring Bengal’s jute, the institute’s sample survey erred by 0.3 per cent, the government’s count by 16.6 per cent. The survey cost a tenth as much. {015-C11}
Yet the man who could measure a crop was, in Menon’s portrait, a prim workaholic who “thought he knew best in practically every matter”. Varma called him a genius “trapped by his own genius”.

The planning state reached far. In 1956, Varma said, a bill set out to license India’s estimated 75 lakh sadhus, and President Rajendra Prasad’s speech to them was, in Varma’s reading, a pitch for the Five-Year Plan.

There was colour, too. JBS Haldane moved to India, he said, because he didn’t want to wear socks anymore. Chintaman Deshmukh, whose sanction of funds kept the institute alive, proposed by inscribing Sanskrit shlokas on a eucalyptus tree.
Shah’s parting pick was David Salsburg’s *The Lady Tasting Tea*, a fun book, he said, even for those who have never done any statistics.

second.label: The German tank problem
second.head: Spies, outnumbered
second.deck: Ajay Shah on how statisticians outguessed the spies about German tanks
body: Late in the Second World War, the Allies wanted to know whether Germany’s new heavy tanks were “a few artisanal demo parts” or were being made at scale. The methodical Germans, Ajay Shah said, numbered every tank in sequence.
So if destroyed tanks bore the numbers 24, 74 and 90, do not conclude that there are only 90. Take the average gap between the numbers and add it to the highest. {#gap}

The spies put production at about 1,500 tanks a month; the statisticians, at about 200. After the war, German production records settled the debate: “the statisticians were right and the humint was wrong”. {015-S01}

quote.text: Just imagine this would have been harder if they had randomized every number.

third.head: Code that made Rao smile
body: Ajay Shah’s closest brush with his hero came through software. His colleague Sourish Das, at the Chennai Mathematical Institute, leads a statistics package written in Julia, a programming language Shah loves.
It offers one way to call many kinds of estimators, from linear regression to random forests, in either frequentist or Bayesian form. {015-R08}
When the team debated names, Das proposed CRRao.jl as “a commitment device”, a way to kick himself into doing it well. Amit Varma approved: “We should have called the show CR Rao.” {015-J06}
Then Rao’s daughter wrote to say she had shown him the package, and he had smiled. “That is the closest that I ever came to the greatness that is CR Rao,” Shah said. {015-S05}

sections.label: The hero
sections.head: An Anand, not a Ramanujan
sections.caption: CR Rao and two kinds of Indian genius
body: Ajay Shah began his PhD without ever having studied probability or statistics, so he was placed in a fourth-year undergraduate econometrics class taught by Dennis Aigner. Aigner’s opening “helicopter tour” of all statistics swept him away.

As Aigner made one estimator better, and then better again, Shah put up his hand: surely there had to be a theoretical limit. Aigner replied that an Indian had asked exactly that question, and answered it. {015-S02}
The answer was the Cramér-Rao lower bound, which CR Rao proved in Calcutta in 1943. His second great result, the Rao-Blackwell theorem, is a technique for making an estimator one step better.
## Two kinds of genius

Shah set Rao against two models of Indian genius. Ramanujan built himself in isolation, but it was GH Hardy and Cambridge that made him one of the world’s great mathematicians. Anand was made by an Indian chess ecosystem, and then nurtured the next generation.

Rao, Shah argued, is the Anand story. He was no precocious child writing letters from afar. He came to the Indian Statistical Institute as a regular student and “exploded in the world created by Mahalanobis”. {015-C06}
Amit Varma added the American Statistical Association’s praise of Rao as “a living legend”, whose work reached fields from economics and genetics to medicine. {015-J22}
~ So, “at the risk of offending Bengalis all over the world”, Shah claimed Rao as the greatest achievement of the Bengal Renaissance.

quote.text: CR Rao to me is a little more of an Anand story and not the Ramanujan story.

sections.label: The head start
sections.head: Credit given, boat missed
sections.caption: credit, founders and a missed boat
body: When work is done in India, Ajay Shah said, the global mainstream very often ignores it. “We see this even today in the age of the internet,” he said. It has happened to him: work of his that was ahead of the mainstream went uncited while others claimed the line. {015-C08}

CR Rao’s results survived because of Ronald Fisher, who understood them on his visits to ISI and began calling them by the joint names. Shah likened those names to a “Darwin-Wallace theory of evolution”. {015-J20}
## The founder’s touch
One Rao convinced a generation at ISI that “this is a game we can play”. The institute was world-class, and its journal, *Sankhya*, was taken by libraries all over the world. {015-J21}
All this happened before independence, without government funding. That, for Shah, is the lesson: excellence comes from an eccentric founder, not from a bureaucracy.

But the head start did not last. From the 1970s, the frontier moved to computational statistics, where, as Shah put it, “an estimator can be an algorithm”. India’s statisticians kept proving theorems, and “didn’t turn on the dime and reinvent themselves”. {015-S04}
~ Amit Varma had a smaller worry: that “you and I will miss the boat on the YouTube algorithm”. {015-J08}

quote.text: Having one CR Rao made a huge difference to a whole generation of statisticians

sections.label: The survivors
sections.head: The bullets that weren’t there
sections.caption: Abraham Wald and the missing bullets
body: Around 1942, Amit Varma said, Abraham Wald was drafted into a wartime research group so brilliant that someone quipped Milton Friedman was the fourth smartest person in the room. Wald had no security clearance; the joke went that a secretary whisked away each sheet as soon as he finished it. {015-J03}
The group was asked how to make planes that came back riddled with bullets stronger. The engines had fewer holes than the fuselage, so the obvious plan was to strengthen the fuselage.
Wald asked where the missing bullets were. If hits are spread evenly, they struck the planes that went down. “So it is the engine that you need to protect.” {015-S06}
Varma found the same insight, arrived at by instinct, in the batsman Ricky Ponting: “Most batsmen have a map of the fielders in their head. I had a map of the gaps.” {015-J19}
## Mind the survivors

Ajay Shah named it survivorship bias. “When you see the data set, you are seeing the survivors,” he said. The ones that died along the way are invisible, so think about where data came from before using it. {015-C03}
~ The same trap, Varma said, makes a fund’s five- or six-year record meaningless: run enough random strategies and one will come out on top by chance.

quote.text: Where are the missing bullets? The missing bullets are in the planes that went down.

sections.label: The bombers
sections.head: The arithmetic of 6,000 feet
sections.caption: how many lives it takes to kill a factory
body: Allied bombers flew from Britain to destroy targets such as oil refineries and tank factories, Ajay Shah said, running into German fighters and the 88-millimetre anti-aircraft gun.
Bombs then fell under gravity alone, Shah said, and the error could run from one kilometre to five. {#cep}

Pilots wanted to fly at 20,000 feet, out of range of the guns. From there, though, very few bombs hit their target. At 6,000 feet more crews would be shot down, but far more bombs would find the factory.
## Counting the cost

The statisticians, a young Robert McNamara among them, set aside the pilots’ fear and asked another question. “How many lives does it take to kill a factory?” Shah said. {015-C10} The answer was 6,000 feet.

The pilots were in uproar: flying that low, they said, was death. In Shah’s telling, McNamara and Curtis LeMay, the head of bomber command, replied: “We love you more than life itself, but we want fewer of you to die.” {015-S08}
~ The damage was checked afterwards by a spotter plane, by local intelligence and, Shah added, by “the brigadier’s girlfriend”. {015-J02}

quote.text: And the brutal answer turns out that you have to fly at 6,000 feet.

sections.label: The professor
sections.head: The man who thought he knew
sections.caption: PC Mahalanobis, sampler and planner
body: PC Mahalanobis trained in physics, Amit Varma said. On the voyage home he was given volumes of the statistics journal *Biometrika*, and by the time he landed in India, statistics was his love.

Reading from Nikhil Menon’s *Planning Democracy*, Varma described a stern, prim workaholic with hair slicked flat by coconut oil, who showed affection only to his pets: dogs, cats and cows. The rest of it, Varma told Ajay Shah, seemed to fit him. “Cows also,” Shah replied. {015-J11}
## The jute test

In 1944 the Bengal government pitted the institute’s random sample survey against plot-by-plot counting of jute, checking both against official sales figures. The count was off by 16.6 per cent, the survey by 0.3 per cent. {015-S11}
Success bred certainty. Milton Friedman, quoted by Varma, warned that able mathematicians, “working in a field of absolutes”, grow dangerous when they turn to economic planning. {015-J23}
Mahalanobis made students and staff record their daily activities in a diary. He, Varma told Shah, “would have loved Aadhaar”. {015-J12}
~ Shah saw a recurring theme: the certainty of science and engineering leaves many successful people unprepared for the complexities of the real world.

quote.text: A man who is a genius, but in a sense is also trapped by his own genius into a hubris and an arrogance

side.boxText: CR Rao was born in 1920 and came to Calcutta from Andhra Pradesh as a young man. Ajay Shah calls him one of the great figures of the 20th century, and the greatest achievement of the Bengal Renaissance. {#greatfigure}

contQuote.text: For too many people, statistics has become a mechanical process where you throw some data into some software package and you get some answers. And always and always it is important to preserve fundamental intuition and insight and common sense.

stories.caption: Chintaman Deshmukh’s proposal
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the official who saved ISI, and his proposal
stories.head: A proposal written on bark
body: Around 1944, a senior government official named Chintaman Deshmukh, later finance minister, approved a flow of funds to the Indian Statistical Institute. It practically guaranteed, Amit Varma said, that the institute would survive.

Varma read from Nikhil Menon’s portrait of him in *Planning Democracy*: a product of Bombay and Cambridge who ranked first in the Indian Civil Service, recited Vedic shlokas for pleasure, translated Kalidasa’s *Meghaduta* from Sanskrit and quoted scripture “to buttress economic policy”.
Varma had never heard of him before, and got curious. Widowed in the early 1950s, Deshmukh had married Durgabai Deshmukh.
She had been married off as a child, at eight. {#eight} At 14, before the marriage was consummated, she told her father she would not go through with it, and the man was liberal enough to let her go.

She was feisty and outspoken, and people were aghast at the marriage: he was sophisticated, while she would say whatever came into her head. Varma searched hard for her autobiography, *Chintaman and I*, found it neither on Kindle nor anywhere else, and at last found a free copy online. {015-R06}

Its opening lines are the proposal: “Chintaman took me to a eucalyptus tree in his garden and inscribed two Sanskrit slokas on its bark. It was a proposal of marriage. I accepted and he kissed me.” {015-S14}
~ Varma asked Ajay Shah whether he had ever inscribed shlokas into the bark of a tree. “No, no such luck,” came the answer. {015-J15}
stories.why: The man who saved a statistics institute was also a romantic, and his wife opened her autobiography with his proposal. Even people who care about statistics and math, Varma concluded, have hearts.
stories.postscript: The funds came around the time Mahalanobis bested the Bengal government’s count. Whether there was a causal link, Varma said, he did not know.

stories.start: So I want to ask you: have you ever heard of the Bharat Sadhu Samaj?
stories.end: which I learned from Nikol's book again, Planning Democracy.
stories.caption: the Bharat Sadhu Samaaj
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how far the planning state reached
stories.head: Licensed to renounce
body: In the mid-1950s, Amit Varma said, India was estimated to have some 75 lakh sadhus. {#sadhus} Many, the thinking went, were frauds and charlatans. How was one to identify a genuine sadhu? “Obviously, the government has to do it.”
So in 1956 a sadhu registration bill was brought in. Anyone wanting to be known as a sadhu would apply to the government for a licence and join the Bharat Sadhu Samaaj.

President Rajendra Prasad then addressed the gathered sadhus: “It is not possible to achieve anything in the other world without setting things in order in this world.” His real subject, Varma said, was the Five-Year Plan. {015-S12}
~ Ajay Shah wanted to know: “Was there a certification examination? Was there a UID?” Varma did not know, but pictured licensed sadhus with their “documentation in triplicate”. {015-J13}

quote.text: You wanna be good in that world, you gotta be good in this world. Five year plan will get you there.

stories.start: JBS Haldane in the mid-50s, when he was in his 60s, had come
stories.end: and Pajama and all of that, but never a sock in sight
stories.caption: Haldane and his socks
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on JBS Haldane, and a lesson for writers
stories.head: The case against socks
body: JBS Haldane came to work at the Indian Statistical Institute in the mid-1950s, in his sixties. Of PC Mahalanobis, always on the move, he said: “The journeyings of our director define a novel random vector.” Amit Varma confessed he had no idea what that meant. {015-J17}
Asked why he had left England for India, Haldane could have said he wanted a simple life, free of convention. Instead he said: “I don’t want to wear socks anymore.” {015-S13}
“Everybody immediately gets a vibe,” Varma said. For him it is a great example of a writing principle, show, don’t tell: “don’t tell something in straight words, show it with something.” {015-C12}
~ In pictures from the rest of his life, Haldane is in banyan, dhoti and pyjama, “but never a sock in sight”.
stories.why: A single concrete detail can carry a whole philosophy of life. Haldane never had to explain his move in abstract words about simplicity or convention; the socks said it, and everyone understood.
stories.postscript: Varma recommends Samanth Subramanian’s *A Dominant Character*, “a great book” on Haldane. {015-R05}

stories.caption: the cricket tipster scam
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on survivorship bias, a con artist’s friend
stories.head: The tipster who can’t lose
body: Amit Varma once wrote a column built on a scam. Write to a thousand people who bet on cricket and offer free tips on the next India–Sri Lanka match. Tell 500 of them India will win, and 500 that Sri Lanka will. {#fivehundred}
Whoever wins, 500 people now know you got it right. Split them, and do it again.
By the time the group is down to ten or twelve, they have seen you call four, five, six results in a row. “They’re willing to pay their money.”

~ Mutual funds can work the same way, Varma said. Run a family of funds on random strategies, and by sheer dumb luck one will come out on top. “But it doesn’t mean that that is a correct strategy. Perhaps it just got lucky.” {015-S07}
stories.why: A great track record means little until you know how many attempts failed and vanished, and selection can look exactly like skill. Ajay Shah’s name for the trap is survivorship bias: the data shows only the survivors. {015-C03}

quiz.q: Spies said 1,500 German tanks a month. What did the statisticians estimate from serial numbers?
quiz.a: About 200 a month, and Germany’s records proved the statisticians right.

quiz.q: What question did Ajay Shah ask in Dennis Aigner’s class that led him to CR Rao?
quiz.a: Whether there must be a theoretical limit on how good an estimator can get.

quiz.q: Which statistician’s decency, Shah said, made sure the world credited Rao’s results to Rao?
quiz.a: Ronald Fisher’s: he began calling the results by the joint names.

quiz.q: Returning planes had fewer holes in the engine. Why did Abraham Wald want the engine protected?
quiz.a: The missing bullets hit planes that never came back, so engine hits were fatal.

quiz.q: In the 1944 Bengal jute contest, how far off were the count and the sample survey?
quiz.a: The count missed by 16.6 per cent; the sample survey by only 0.3.

quiz.q: Why, by his own account, did JBS Haldane leave England for India?
quiz.a: He simply said that he didn’t want to wear socks anymore.
